item.title: Combinatorial optimization with bounded subdeterminants
item.description: arXiv:2611.13065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We take a first step toward a broader study of classical combinatorial optimization problems through the maximum subdeterminants of their standard integer programming formulations, yielding new positive results for several famous (NP-hard) problems. An integer matrix is totally $\Delta$-modular if every square submatrix has determinant of absolute value at most $\Delta$. For every fixed $\Delta$, it has been known that maximum clique, maximum stable set, and minimum vertex cover can be solved in polynomial time on instances for which the coefficient matrix of the natural formulation is totally $\Delta$-modular. We extend this list by showing that the same holds for many other problems, including the weighted versions of maximum cut, the traveling salesman problem, feedback vertex set, odd cycle transversal, dominating set, max 2-sat, induced matching, and cluster vertex deletion, as well as for $k$-colorability and graph isomorphism. Our proofs reveal several new ways in which bounded subdeterminants impose combinatorial structure: they bound the size or maximum degree of the input graph, bound packings of cycles and other obstructions, or yield decompositions into tractable graph classes such as forests, chordal graphs, graphs of bounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded linear mim-width.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Fiorini, J. Pascal Gollin, Tony Huynh, Simon Keil, O-joung Kwon, Sang-il Oum, Roohani Sharma, Stefan Weltge

item.title: A Fast Algorithm for Subspace Convolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.13134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A cornerstone result in Boolean lattice theory is the subset-zeta transform, which computes the $f$-weighted subset summation problem $(Z f)(B)=\sum_{A\subseteq B}f(A)$ for all $ B\subseteq[n]$ in $O(N \log N)$ additions instead of the na\"ive $O(3^n) = O(N^{\log_2 3})$, where $N=2^n$. This paper studies the algebraic analogue of this problem--the subspace summation problem--where subsets are replaced by linear subspaces in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Surprisingly, we show that this problem admits a similar $\Theta_q(N_q \log N_q)$-time algorithm, where $N_q$ is the number of subspaces. This improves substantially (in both theory and practice) over lattice-based algorithms ([BHK+16, KKW16]), which are known to be optimal for addition-only algorithms over $\mathbb R$. We prove similar runtimes for inversion, rank-constrained sums and span convolution. We describe two main applications: Fast linear algebra on Grassmann graphs: Matrix--vector multiplication for arbitrary distance-invariant kernels on $N$-vertex Grassmann graphs in $O_q(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations, together with fast spectral projections and exact solutions of the corresponding linear systems. Graph coloring of low binary cut-rank graphs: An $n^{2^{r^2/4+O(1)}}$-time algorithm for computing the chromatic number and chromatic polynomial of an $n$-vertex graph, given a rank-decomposition of width $r$. We also give quantitative reductions from satisfiability and monotone constraint problems. Experiments show speedups in measured running time of up to $18$ over the covering-pair algorithm for the zeta transform, $190$ over Poisson summation for rank-constrained sums, and $22$ over the distance-matrix recurrence for Grassmann kernel multiplication. Lean 4 formalizations of the transform identities, arithmetic operation bounds, and graph-coloring constructions accompany the paper [PW26].
item.dc:creator: Shlomo A. Perles, Omri Weinstein

item.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
item.description: arXiv:2611.13224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.
item.dc:creator: S. Rasoul Etesami

item.title: Function Inversion Reporting
item.description: arXiv:2611.13294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the Function Inversion problem, the goal is to invert a function $f:[N] \to [N]$ in two phases. In the preprocessing phase, the offline algorithm computes an advice string of length $S$ bits. In the online phase, the online algorithm receives the advice and a challenge $y \in [N]$, and the goal is to find a preimage $x \in [N]$ such that $f(x) = y$ in time $T$. The problem was initially studied in cryptography, but in recent years it has found various applications to data structure problems. Yet, several of the applications require a variant of Function Inversion, known as Function Inversion Reporting, where the goal is to output all preimages of the challenge $y$. In this paper, we study the Function Inversion Reporting problem in a systematic way by unifying and improving existing algorithms. As a result, we obtain improved data structures for several problems including 3SUM-Indexing Reporting, Range Reporting, Approximate Nearest Neighbor, Jumbled Indexing Reporting, and Gapped String Indexing Reporting.
item.dc:creator: Itai Dinur, Alexander Golovnev, Chao Yan, Yiding Zhu

item.title: Minimum Membership Dominating Set and Its Generalization: Leafage vs. Asteroidal Number
item.description: arXiv:2611.13392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Dominating Set problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by leafage, a structural graph parameter defined on chordal graphs. We investigate whether this tractability extends to its variants with natural constraints. Specifically, we study the Minimum Membership Dominating Set problem and its generalization, the Min. $(\sigma, \rho)$-Dominating Set problem. Given a graph $G$ and a positive integer $\ell$, Minimum Membership Dominating Set asks whether there is a dominating set $D$ such that every vertex in $G$ is dominated by at most $\ell$ vertices in $D$. We first show a negative result: Minimum Membership Dominating Set parameterized by leafage plus $\ell$ is W[1]-hard, demonstrating that even this natural constraint serves as a severe barrier to designing FPT algorithms. To complement this, we present an XP algorithm for the Min. $(\sigma, \rho)$-Dominating Set problem parameterized by asteroidal number plus $\mu$, where $\sigma$ and $\rho$ are finite sets of non-negative integers and $\mu$ is the maximum value in $\sigma \cup \rho$. Note that asteroidal number generalizes leafage to arbitrary graphs. Combining this algorithm with our structural bound that every graph $G$ admits a dominating set such that no vertex is dominated by more than $7\mathsf{an}(G)-6$ vertices, where $\mathsf{an}(G)$ denotes the asteroidal number of $G$, we show that Minimum Membership Dominating Set admits an XP algorithm parameterized solely by asteroidal number.
item.dc:creator: Yuma Tamura, Daichi Wakayama, Akira Suzuki, Xiao Zhou

item.title: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.13568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tokenisers such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) shorten text by repeatedly merging an adjacent pair of symbols into a new one; fewer tokens mean less computation. We ask whether an efficient algorithm can choose $k$ merges that leave a string of length $n$ almost as short as possible; doing nothing is already within a factor $n$. We prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm comes within a factor $c\,n/\log n$, for some constant $c>0$, already for one binary string and for BPE-style merges that replace every occurrence. The key idea is that $k$ merges form a grammar with $k$ rules: a vertex-cover gap becomes a grammar-size gap, which we amplify with relabelled copies, encode in binary and realise with explicit merges. For merges that may skip occurrences, a simple algorithm achieves $O(n/\log\log n)$, and no Karp reduction can prove hardness beyond order $n/\log n$ unless coNP $\subseteq$ NP/poly. Over a one-letter alphabet, both tokenisation problems left open by Kastreva et al. are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Improved Bounds for Online Matching with Random Edge Arrivals
item.description: arXiv:2611.13571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the unweighted online matching problem with random edge arrivals, where each edge arrives at an independent time drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject it while maintaining a matching. Guruganesh and Singla (IPCO, 2017) first broke the $1/2$ barrier of the naive Greedy algorithm by giving a $(1/2+\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm for a small constant $\varepsilon>0$, a guarantee that has remained the best known for nearly a decade. We give a simple three-phase algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $0.5445$ by deliberately rejecting selected early edges to reserve their endpoints for later matching opportunities. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm is $0.5535$-competitive on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs. We also establish competitive ratio upper bounds below $0.6964$ for general graphs and $0.7043$ for bipartite graphs via exact rational evaluation of an optimal-policy recurrence on fixed graphs, even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism.
item.dc:creator: Yilong Feng, Haolong Li, Zonghan Yang

item.title: Greedy+Singleton for knapsack-constrained monotone submodular maximization has approximation ratio exactly $\beta^\star \approx 0.42944$
item.description: arXiv:2611.13575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Greedy+Singleton is the textbook heuristic for monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint: it returns the better of the cost-benefit greedy set and the best single item. Its worst-case approximation ratio, known only to lie in $[0.427, 0.42945]$ (Feldman-Nutov-Shoham; Kulik-Schwartz-Shachnai), is exactly an explicit constant $\beta^\star\approx 0.42944$. In the extremal instances, many cheap "filler" items wear down the value of two large optimal items while greedy spends the budget, until neither fits. This picture gives a sharper factor-revealing relaxation; we bound it analytically near the extremal parameters, up to finitely many interval-arithmetic checks, and certify it elsewhere by an exact branch-and-bound. The matching bad instances are tie-free and checkable by hand. For the version that stops at the first item that does not fit, Wolsey's bound $1-e^{-\beta_W}\approx 0.35780$, where $e^{\beta_W}=2-\beta_W$, is tight; Wolsey stated this for his variant without giving the instances, and we give an explicit family with no ties that also covers comparison with the best feasible singleton. The CELF rule also has ratio exactly $\beta^\star$.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Approximating graphic TSP by b-matchings
item.description: arXiv:2611.13585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for graphic TSP that returns a tour of length at most $\frac{89}{64}=\frac{7}{5}-\frac{3}{320}$ times the value of the subtour relaxation. This improves the long-standing ratio $\frac75$ of Seb\H{o} and Vygen and shows that the integrality gap of the subtour LP on graphic instances is at most $\frac{89}{64}\approx 1.3906$. We optimize a non-linear objective function over an odd-join polytope, which uses (i) a new removable system of edges, and (ii) reconnection of subtours if the graph is disconnected. This approach gives a $\frac{13}{10}$-approximation algorithm for $4$-regular $4$-vertex-connected graphs, improving the $\frac43$ of Newman, and a $\frac43$-approximation for $k$-vertex-connected graphs of maximum degree at most $k+1$, for every $k\ge 3$. For the general graphic TSP, we construct a feasible point in the odd-join polytope, using an optimal vertex from the Subtour linear programming relaxation of TSP, which helps us bound the approximation factor by 89/64.
item.dc:creator: Swati Gupta, Mehrdad Sohrabi, Levent Tun\c{c}el

item.title: Min-CSPs on Complete Instances III: Nearly Optimal Characterizations of Approximation for Symmetric CSPs
item.description: arXiv:2611.13635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies complete Min-$k$-CSPs: an instance on $n$ variables has one nontrivial constraint for every $k$-set of variables (so $\binom{n}{k}$ constraints in total), and the goal is to find an assignment that minimizes the number of unsatisfied constraints. They are motivated by the connections to machine learning and data science, as well as the possibility of being testbeds for new algorithmic techniques. Previous recent results presented polynomial-time algorithms for the decision version of every complete Boolean $k$-CSP, which is a necessary condition for any multiplicative approximations for the minimization version, but nontrivial approximation results have been limited to fragile CSPs, 2-SAT, and NAE-3-SAT, leaving the approximability of most complete Boolean Min-CSPs open, including complete Min-$k$-SAT. In this paper, we resolve this question, up to nearly matching factors, for the natural class of symmetric Boolean predicates. Given $A \subseteq \{0, \dots, k\}$, Min-CSP($A$) is a Min-$k$-CSP where each constraint is specified by $k$ literals and is satisfied if the number of true literals belongs to $A$. Let $w(A)$ be the maximum number of consecutive integers in $A$. Our main results for complete Min-CSP($A$) are (1) a QPTAS for $w(A) \leq 2$ and (2) an $\widetilde{O}(n^{w(A)-3})$-approximation for $w(A) \geq 3$, as well as almost matching hardness results for the latter. Our QPTAS for $w(A)=2$ significantly improves the previous $O(1)$-approximation for Min-2-SAT and the $\operatorname{polylog}(n)$-approximation for Min-NAE-3-SAT, as well as extends the PTAS for fragile CSPs (i.e., $w(A) = 1$).
item.dc:creator: Yihwan Chae, Chenglin Fan, Donghyeon Lee, Euiwoong Lee

item.title: List Update with Per-Page Maximum Delay
item.description: arXiv:2611.13750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study list update with per-page maximum delay. Requests may wait, and one access clears all pending requests of a page at its current list rank, paying their maximum waiting penalty. Each service can change the permutation and therefore the cost of later accesses. We give a strictly $5$-competitive deterministic algorithm: serve a page when the oldest waiting time reaches two thirds of its current rank, then move it to the front. Our main tool is an asynchronous marked-rank coupling that compares different list orders and different service histories. A temporal transfer principle separates this permutation argument from two waiting-cost inequalities. It gives factor $5$ for page-specific superadditive penalties, common calendar rates, and additional hard deadlines; deadlines alone admit factor $3$. Two structural conditions on request-specific penalties give factor $3+2\kappa$. In particular, nonincreasing request severity retains factor $5$ even with unbounded weight ratios. For linear delay, offline optimization is NP-complete but fixed-parameter tractable in the number of pages. We characterize fixed-list batching, show an $\Omega(m)$ gap between the best static order and dynamic reordering, and prove that the optimal deterministic factor for one page is exactly $2$. Counterexamples delineate the threshold rule's scope.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu

item.title: Stochastic Aggregation with Prescribed Resources and Additive Delay
item.description: arXiv:2611.13757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online aggregation with prescribed resources and additive delay. In this problem, we are given a finite set of resources with purchase costs and a collection of request types, each specifying the resources it requires. Requests arrive over time, and each request can be served immediately or postponed to a later time. A service may serve several pending requests together by purchasing every resource required by at least one of them, paying for each purchased resource only once. These purchases serve only the current batch; resources needed in a later service must be purchased again. A request served $t$ units of time after its arrival incurs delay cost $t$. The objective is to serve all requests while minimizing the sum of resource purchase costs and individual delay costs. We consider a stochastic version of this problem in which requests of each type follow an independent Poisson process of known rate. An online algorithm knows these rates but observes requests only upon arrival. We compare its expected cost with that of an offline optimum that knows the entire realized input and may choose every batch freely. A resource--scale linear program supplies both an offline lower certificate and synchronized service periods. This yields a deterministic online algorithm with polynomial-time preprocessing on rational input and a long-run ratio of expectations below $2.113$. The guarantee applies in particular to rooted multi-level aggregation and prescribed-pair aggregation on trees. Besides, for Poisson TCP acknowledgment, we further characterize the optimal long-run ratio of expectations at every load, showing that its worst-case value is approximately 1.409 and is attained by a deterministic online policy.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu

item.title: Online Network Design with Additive Delays and Poisson Arrivals
item.description: arXiv:2611.13859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online service systems in which requests arrive at locations in a network. A service may open a facility and connect customers, buy a subtree linking them to a root, or send a mobile server to visit them. Combining requests can save opening, network, or travel costs, but each request pays its own waiting time. The objective is the sum of these spatial costs and individual delays. We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates. The algorithms know how often requests occur, but observe them only upon arrival. We show that these rates suffice to make fixed spatial choices that compete with an offline optimum free to adapt to the realized input. We obtain long-run ratios of expectations below $27.249$ for facility location in finite metrics, $94.415$ for multi-root aggregation on trees, and $24.326$ for online service on trees. All three algorithms are deterministic; the multi-root algorithm also has polynomial-time preprocessing on rational inputs. The proofs connect rate-based spatial choices with lower bounds on unavoidable purchase, movement, and waiting costs. All main proofs are self-contained, and every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu

item.title: Online Network Design with Maximum Delay and Stochastic Arrivals
item.description: arXiv:2611.13865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online network services that combine pending requests into batches. Each batch pays for its spatial service and for the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is the sum of these costs over all batches. Thus requests can share both a spatial purchase and one maximum-delay charge. We assume independent Poisson arrivals of known rates, while actual requests are revealed only upon arrival. For stateless services, suppose that each type has an attainable minimum cost when served alone, that every batch costs at least the stand-alone minimum of each type it contains, and that one finite-cost action can serve any batch, regardless of its request multiplicities. We give a deterministic algorithm with long-run ratio of expectations $e/(e-1)$ against an unrestricted offline optimum. This factor is optimal, even allowing randomization, already at one request location. The key comparison measures the union of time intervals associated with requests. The theorem applies directly to multi-root and pair aggregation on trees. We also study facility location, where each request pays its own connection distance and the bounded-action assumption can fail. A deterministic policy gives a ratio $3$ for arbitrary nonnegative opening costs. It immediately serves a finite initial set of requests, computes an assignment from their observed arrival gaps, and then keeps that assignment fixed. Its analysis combines Poisson insertion with a time-slice packing bound on the offline optimum. Every guarantee includes the full cost of completing finite inputs without an end-of-input signal.
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu

item.title: Real-Time String Indexing in Optimal Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.13950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we describe the first fully real-time indexing solution for pattern matching over an arbitrary integer alphabet. Our data structure spends $O(1)$ worst-case time w.h.p. for processing each new letter appended to $T$ and worst-case $O(|P|+occ)$ time for reporting all occurrences of $P$, where $T$ and $P$ are strings over an integer alphabet. The main idea of our solution is a novel representation of the suffix tree, the path-decomposed suffix tree, which does not store the full topology of the suffix tree but instead decomposes it into paths, each stored in a dictionary that encodes parent--child relationships indirectly.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Kucherov, Yakov Nekrich

item.title: What to Predict for Efficient Scheduling on Parallel Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.13980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for scheduling on multiple parallel machines under the objectives of minimizing the makespan or the total weighted completion time. We assume that the algorithm has access to noisy information (the prediction) about an optimal solution, expressed through a solution encoding that implicitly quantifies both the amount of information provided and the nature of noise (errors in the prediction). Our central question is to determine the maximum level of noise that still allows for efficiently recovering this optimal solution. We observe that information guiding greedy scheduling to optimality or revealing the optimal assignment of tasks to machines is very sensitive to noise, and prove that recovering an optimal solution from solution encodings capturing either is computationally hard, even for a small (non-constant) number of errors. On the positive side, we show that an order-based encoding, which leads to errors that are dispersed locally, is robust to noise. We present a dynamic programming framework that utilizes this encoding and solves optimally several classical scheduling problems, including makespan and total weighted completion time minimization on identical or unrelated machines.
item.dc:creator: Evripidis Bampis, Bruno Escoffier, Dimitris Fotakis, Giorgos Mitropoulos, Michalis Xefteris

item.title: Bounded Weighted Edit Distance with Metric Costs
item.description: arXiv:2611.13984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic $O(n+k^2)$-time algorithm for bounded weighted edit distance when the input costs form an integer metric on the alphabet extended by a gap symbol. Here $n$ is the total input length and $k$ is the given threshold on the distance. If the distance is at most $k$, the algorithm returns it with an optimal alignment. Otherwise, it reports that the distance exceeds $k$. The running time matches the classical unit-cost bound and is independent of the alphabet size and of the largest cost. The algorithm keeps only the farthest-reaching prefix alignment for each cost and each difference between the total gap costs of the aligned prefixes. For real metrics whose nonzero costs are at least one, scaling and upward rounding give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for the bounded problem in $\widetilde{O}(n+(k/\varepsilon)^2)$ time. If insertions and deletions have integer costs, the running time improves to $\widetilde{O}(n+k^2/\varepsilon)$.
item.dc:creator: Jihan Wang

item.title: Nonadaptive One-Sided Testing of Binary Rank
item.description: arXiv:2611.14163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition its one-entries. We study entry-query testing of binary rank at most $d$, with one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. We give a tester using $\tilde O(d^4/\epsilon^2)$ queries, independent of the matrix dimensions and a general lower bound of $\tilde \Omega(d^{3/2}/\epsilon)$.
item.dc:creator: Nader H. Bshouty

item.title: Directed Singular-Value Sparsifiers with $O(n \log n/\epsilon^2)$ Arcs
item.description: arXiv:2611.14342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an unweighted directed graph, a sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs that preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. In this work, we study singular-value sparsifiers, which are generalizations of spectral sparsifiers. Singular-value sparsifiers find a number of applications in theoretical computer science, such as maintaining directed cuts and flows, speeding up directed Laplacian solvers, and sparsifying dense weight matrices in neural networks. Strong singular-value (SV) approximation supports sparse representations of directed random walks with guarantees that remain stable under products, and controls bilinear error in the left and right Schur-complement metrics. We prove that every unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices admits an $\varepsilon$-SV sparsifier with $O(n\log(2n)/\varepsilon^2)$ arcs, improving the $O(n\log^5 n/\varepsilon^2)$ support bound of Lau, Wang, and Zhou. The sparsifier is a nonnegative reweighting of original arcs and preserves every in-degree and out-degree exactly. We also give a randomized construction with $\tilde{O}(m+n)$ real-arithmetic running time, where $m$ is the input support size, and the output has the same support bound and rational weights of polynomial bit length.
item.dc:creator: Emile Anand

item.title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.14513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.
item.dc:creator: Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hirotaka Yoneda, Masataka Yoneda

item.title: 51 Additions per Recursive Step for Rank-23 $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication, Machine-Checked over Arbitrary Rings
item.description: arXiv:2611.12907v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a rank-23 bilinear scheme for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication that uses 51 additions per recursive step in the alternative-basis (Karstadt-Schwartz) cost model, one below Nielsen's 52 (arXiv:2609.06588). The count 51 itself was first posted, on a different scheme, by Stapleton and Perminov (arXiv:2609.32388), found by heuristic sparse-basis search; the present work is independent and complementary: exactness and breadth rather than a single construction. The scheme is valid over every ring, so it recurses on block matrices, and its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4/Mathlib. The count is exactly optimal for the scheme's equivalence class: we introduce an exact free-basis minimization procedure whose negative answers are exhaustion proofs, and use it to show that 51 is the minimum for this class, that 52 is exactly optimal both for Nielsen's class and for the class of the current flat-model record, and to sweep the complete Heule-Kauers-Seidl database of rank-23 classes. The sweep is complete: exactly four classes attain 51, all in a single HKS invariant family. We machine-check Stapleton and Perminov's scheme as well, and prove in Lean that their 51 is optimal for its class. Separately, we document a systematic gap between $\mathbb{F}_2$ and signed optima: the $\mathbb{F}_2$-optimal chains of a class typically admit no sign assignment under most of the class's integer sign models, and certificate lifting fails where a direct signed search succeeds.
item.dc:creator: Greg Sidebottom

item.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
item.description: arXiv:2611.13061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Parameterized Complexity and Geometric Approximation of Riesz Energy Subset Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.13600v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We choose $k$ of $n$ sites to minimize Riesz $s$-energy, in which a pair at distance $t$ contributes $t^{-s}$. For $s=2$, exact selection is polynomial on a line but NP-hard in the plane. Adapting the proxy lemma of Ceccarello et al. gives an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) for fixed Euclidean dimension and fixed $s>0$. To sharpen the bound, we start with a geometric packing. Farthest-first traversal gives $2k$ centers separated by at least the last insertion distance $r$. If one site of an optimum is removed, each of the $k-1$ remaining sites excludes at most one center closer than $r/2$, leaving at least $k+1$ centers free. The new step is a discrete exchange bound: the removed site's interaction energy is at most the average it would contribute at those free centers. In the plane at $s=2$, this reduces the representative bound from $O(k^2\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$ for a packing estimate of total energy to $O(k\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$, independently of $n$. Rational planar examples show that the resulting separation scale $r/\sqrt{\log(2k)}$ is sharp. A $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation on rational planar sites takes $O(nk+n\log n)+(C\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)^k$ operations of polynomial bit cost. The observed number $M$ of representatives determines the search size $\binom{M}{k}$. With one million sites, $k=5$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, the exchange grid left 252 subsets on clustered inputs and about $9.3\times10^{26}$ on uniform inputs. The method extends to metrics of bounded doubling dimension and to compact domains with effective geometric routines, including filled simple polygons. At $s=2$, exact decision on metrics with nonzero distances in $\{1,2\}$ is W[1]-complete in $k$. A gap that shrinks with $k$ rules out a deterministic EPAS on unrestricted metrics unless FPT = W[1].
item.dc:creator: Michael Emmerich (Faculty of Information Technology, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a, Finland), Soumen Atta (Faculty of Information Technology, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a, Finland)

item.title: Mixed-integer dual network problems are solvable in strongly polynomial time
item.description: arXiv:2611.14045v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper we show that mixed-integer linear programming is solvable in strongly polynomial time if the constraint matrix is totally unimodular with at most two nonzero entries in every row. This is done by reducing the problem to an instance of minimization of an $L$-convex function.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Zambelli

item.title: Bounding and Approximating Kostka Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.14322v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kostka numbers, the coefficients of Schur polynomials, count semistandard Young tableaux of prescribed shape and weight. We give a deterministic algorithm for approximating Kostka numbers within a simply exponential factor in the number of variables and the size of the partition. Our approach combines Gurvits capacity bounds for log-concave polynomials with an algorithm for approximating the Gurvits capacity of a Schur polynomial. For a Schur polynomial in $n$ variables indexed by $\lambda$, we show that the logarithm of the capacity associated with any nonzero coefficient can be approximated to additive error $\epsilon$ in time polynomial in $n$, $|\lambda|$, and $\log(1/\epsilon)$. The analysis establishes an explicit bounded optimization region and efficient approximate first-order oracles, and handles boundary weights through a factorization into smaller Schur polynomials.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Leake, Zirou Zhang

item.title: A note on the intractability of enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression
item.description: arXiv:2611.14471v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that, given a Horn expression and a family of inclusion-wise maximal satisfiable subsets of its clauses, deciding whether there exists another maximal satisfiable subset is NP-complete. As a consequence, unless P=NP, there is no output-polynomial time algorithm enumerating the maximal satisfiable subformulas of a Horn expression.
item.dc:creator: Oscar Defrain, Corentin Jazeron, Kazuhisa Makino

item.title: Convex Minimization with Integer Minima in $\widetilde O(n^4)$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2304.03426v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given a convex function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose set of minimizers is nonempty and closed, lies in a box of radius $R$ with $\log R\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and has integral extreme points, we give a randomized algorithm that finds an integral minimizer of $f$ with high probability using $O(n^2\log n+n\log R)$ calls to a separation oracle, $O(n+\log R/\log n)$ calls to an approximate shortest vector routine such as the LLL algorithm, and $O(n^4\log(nR)\log\log n)$ other arithmetic operations. The previous best polynomial time algorithm [Jiang, SODA 2021, JACM 2022] achieves $O(n(n\log\log n/\log n+\log R))$ oracle complexity, but its overall runtime is at least $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^8)$. We obtain our speedup by combining a variant of the volumetric center cutting plane method of [Vaidya, FOCS 1989], run on the hybrid barrier of [Lee, Sidford, Wong, FOCS 2015] with the fast implementation of [Jiang, Lee, Song, Wong, STOC 2020], and a variant of the LLL algorithm that reduces segments of consecutive basis vectors recursively. The method runs in blocks, so that shortest vectors are computed only $O(n+\log R/\log n)$ times, and each computation takes $O(n^3\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations in exact arithmetic. For submodular function minimization, our result implies an algorithm using $O(n^3\log n)$ calls to an evaluation oracle and $O(n^4\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations in total. Its oracle complexity is better than that of the algorithms of [Lee, Sidford, Wong, FOCS 2015] and [Dadush, V\'egh, Zambelli, SODA 2018, MOR 2021], which had the best running time before this work.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Jiang, Yin Tat Lee, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Differentially Private Verification of Distribution Properties
item.description: arXiv:2604.10819v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A recent line of work initiated by Chiesa and Gur and further developed by Herman and Rothblum investigates the sample and communication complexity of verifying properties of distributions with the assistance of a powerful, knowledgeable, but untrusted prover. In this work, we initiate the study of differentially private distribution property verification. After all, if we do not trust the prover to help us with verification, why should we trust it with our sensitive sample? We map a landscape of differentially private verification of properties of distributions. In the non-private case it is known that one-round private-coin protocols can have substantially lower complexity than public-coin (AM) protocols. In contrast, the possibility for improvement in differentially private interactive proofs depends on the privacy parameter regime and model. Drawing on connections between privacy and replicability and privacy amplification techniques in the literature we show: 1. There exists a reduction from any one-round $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private private-coin protocol to a differentially private AM protocol for the parameter regime $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{s})$ and $\delta= O(1/s^{5/2})$ with approximately the same privacy and sample and communication complexities. In the local model, this is relaxed to $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{\log s})$ 2. However, when the privacy guarantee is very relaxed ($\varepsilon \in \Omega(\log s)$), private coins indeed reduce sample and communication complexities. We also obtain a computationally efficient Merlin-Arthur proof for privately testing whether samples are drawn from a product distribution and prove that its sample complexity is optimal up to a $polylog N$ factor by reducing uniformity testing to independence testing with Boolean attributes and appealing to known lower bounds on sample complexity for private uniformity testing.
item.dc:creator: Elbert Du, Cynthia Dwork, Pranay Tankala, Linjun Zhang

item.title: Layer-Based Width for PAFP
item.description: arXiv:2605.12457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Path Avoiding Forbidden Pairs problem (PAFP) asks whether, in a directed graph $G$ with two of its vertices labeled $s,t$ and a set $\mathcal F$ of forbidden vertex pairs, there is an $s$--$t$ path that contains at most one endpoint from each pair in $\mathcal F$. We initiate the study of PAFP through a layer-based width measure. We first look at the directed union digraph $G\cup\mathcal F$, which is obtained by adding one arc per forbidden pair to $G$, oriented according to a fixed reachability-compatible order. Let the BFS layer $L_d$ be the set of vertices at directed shortest-path distance $d$ from $s$, and define the BFS-width from $s$ as $\max_d |L_d|$. We show that if $G\cup\mathcal F$ has BFS-width $b$ from $s$, and $p$ is the maximum, over BFS-layer cuts, of the smaller of the numbers of distinct heads and distinct tails of backward arcs crossing the cut, then PAFP is FPT parameterized by $b+p$. Here a backward arc goes from a later BFS layer to an earlier one. In contrast, we show that bounded BFS-width alone does not suffice: PAFP remains $\mathsf{NP}$-complete when the union digraph has BFS-width 2. We also study layer-based width parameters on the input graph. We show that if the input DAG has BFS-width at most $2$ and only $k$ backward input arcs, then PAFP can be decided in $2^k |I|^{O(1)}$ time, with unrestricted forbidden pairs, and this result is tight. Moreover, we study exact-length layers in the input graph, where the $d$-th exact-length layer consists of the vertices reachable from $s$ by a directed path of length exactly $d$. We show that for DAGs of exact-length width at most $2$, PAFP is polynomial-time decidable by a $2$-SAT encoding of fixed-length paths. Unlike previously known polynomial-time regimes our 2 input -graph tractability results simultaneously allow unrestricted forbidden pairs and input graphs with exponentially many $s$--$t$ paths.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 37th International Workshop on Combinatorial Algorithms (IWOCA 2026), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16587, pp. 311-326, Springer (2026)
item.dc:creator: Samuel German

item.title: Sliding-Window Quotas in Apache Hadoop YARN: Exact Admission and Flexible Placement
item.description: arXiv:2606.06145v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A reservation in Apache Hadoop YARN can pass a quota of 600 MiB-hours even when a 24-hour window contains 720 MiB-hours of usage. YARN subtracts sampled prefixes to estimate the window total. This can also reject requests that fit, and adding demand can introduce a sample that reverses a rejection. We bound the peak error in both directions and implement an exact check that visits rate changes at either edge of the window. When the two policies see the same history in replays from two public job traces, they disagree on up to $13.3\%$ of requests. Among requests both policies admit, the 95th-percentile latency of inserting a reservation into the plan is $39$--$47\%$ of the sampled baseline. A separate linear scan finds all feasible integer starts for a single constant-demand stage. In a ResourceManager test, the default agent rejects a flexible request. The ResourceManager accepts the stage when submitted at a start found by the scan. In one replay, committing such retries reduces total admissions.
item.dc:creator: Ruize Zhao

item.title: Query Complexity of Testing Structured Parenthesis Languages
item.description: arXiv:2609.37431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the query complexity of testing membership in structured string languages, focusing on Dyck languages and natural generalizations. A tester receives query access to a word and must distinguish valid inputs from words that are far in Hamming distance, while inspecting only a sublinear number of positions. Our results sharpen the boundary between constant-query testability and polynomial query complexity. First, we prove an $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ lower bound for testing Dyck languages $D_m$ with any fixed number $m\ge2$ of parenthesis types, improving the previous $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ lower bound of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA `18) and nearly matching their upper bound of $O(n^{2/5+o(1)})$. Furthermore, we show that all nonadaptive algorithms for these problems require $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ queries. Our lower bounds use a P\'olya-urn process to construct the hard distribution; Second, we identify a broad class of weighted-parenthesis languages, which we call {\em excursion languages,} that remain constant-query testable. These languages encode bounded-step walks that stay nonnegative and return to zero. For every fixed excursion language, we give a nonadaptive tester with query complexity $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$, and we prove this dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal, even for adaptive algorithms. As a special case, we obtain the tight $\Theta(1/\varepsilon^2)$ query complexity of testing $D_1$, improving the previous $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2)$ upper bound and giving the first matching two-sided-error lower bound. Third, we construct a simple hard language, Hidden String, that is generated by a deterministic linear grammar but nevertheless requires $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ adaptive queries and $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ nonadaptive queries to test. This shows that polynomial query complexity appears even for highly restricted string languages.
item.dc:creator: Tim Jackman, Diptaksho Palit, Sofya Raskhodnikova

item.title: Edit Distance Approximation: Subquadratic Factor Three and Monge Approximation Schemes
item.description: arXiv:2610.01311v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The weighted edit distance $\mathsf{ed}^w(X,Y)$ is the minimum cost of an alignment of strings $X$ and $Y$, where a weight function $w$ specifies the cost of each character insertion, deletion, and substitution. For strings of total length $N$, the textbook dynamic program takes $O(N^2)$ time, and no $O(N^{2-\delta})$-time algorithm exists, even for unit costs, unless the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis (OVH) fails. This motivates the study of approximation algorithms. For unit costs and metric weights, the best truly subquadratic approximation factor was $3+\varepsilon$; we give randomized $3$-approximations in $\tilde O(N^{11/6})$ and $\tilde O(N^{40/21})$ time, respectively. For non-metric weights, we prove quadratic lower bounds for any approximation factor: $\Omega(N^2)$ queries to $w$ over alphabets of size $\Theta(N)$, and OVH-hardness over constant-size alphabets. These lower bounds motivate the bounded setting, parameterized by $k:=\mathsf{ed}^w(X,Y)$ for $w$ normalized so that every edit costs at least one. We give a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm in $\tilde O(N+k^2/\sqrt\varepsilon)$ time, matching the $O(N+k^2)$-time Landau-Vishkin algorithm for unit costs up to logarithmic factors for constant $\varepsilon>0$. Our main technical contribution is a Monge-matrix approximation framework for alignment problems: every $n\times n$ Monge matrix with entries in $\{0\}\cup[1,W]$ has an entrywise $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation by a Monge matrix with $\tilde O(n\log(W)/\sqrt\varepsilon)$ strict Monge inequalities. As further applications of our Monge approximation framework, we maintain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of $\mathsf{ed}^w(X,Y)$ under character edits in $\tilde O(N\log(W)/\sqrt\varepsilon)$ time per update for weights at most $W$, and in $\tilde O(K/\sqrt\varepsilon)$ time for a fixed threshold $K$.
item.dc:creator: Egor Gorbachev

item.title: Bounded Integer Programming in Almost $N^{2d}$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.25955v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study integer programs in standard form $\min\{\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\mathbf{l}\leq\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{u},\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$, where $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times n}$, all entries of $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{l},\mathbf{u}$ are integers, and every variable bound is finite. Let $N$ be an upper bound on the absolute values of the entries of $A$, and $c_{\max}$ one on the absolute values of the costs. For every fixed $d$ and every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ we give a deterministic algorithm running in time \[ T_{\textrm LP}+O_d(n)+O_{d,\varepsilon}\bigl(N^{2d+\varepsilon}\log^2(c_{\max}+2)\bigr), \] where $T_{\textrm LP}$ is the time to solve one linear programming relaxation exactly. Prior to our work, the best known running time for bounded variables was $N^{O(d^2)}$ [Eisenbrand \& Weismantel'20], and it has been a fundamental open problem whether the exponent $O(d^2)$ can be improved to one linear in $d$. We answer this question affirmatively, with the exponent $2d+\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao, Guochuan Zhang

item.title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
item.description: arXiv:2610.35495v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $\Theta(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Heged\"{u}s 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $\Theta(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.
item.dc:creator: Hadley Black, Arya Mazumdar, Barna Saha, Geelon So

item.title: Deterministic $n^{O(\log n)}$ Graph Isomorphism Algorithm via Inherited Decompositions
item.description: arXiv:2611.01399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic $n^{O(\log d)}$-time algorithm for isomorphism of graphs with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $d$. Since $d<n$, this is an $n^{O(\log n)}$-time algorithm for graph isomorphism. To our knowledge, this is the first proof of such a worst-case bound for general graphs. It improves the explicit cubic logarithmic exponent in the analysis of the corrected Luks--Babai algorithm. For graphs of maximum degree $d$, the best previous bound known to us, due to Grohe, Neuen, and Schweitzer, is $n^{O((\log d)^c)}$ for an absolute constant $c$. The algorithm uses the local-certificate and color-refinement steps of Babai's quasipolynomial algorithm, but retains the decomposition of each recursive instance when it solves an auxiliary coloring problem. There are two reasons for retaining this information. First, a local test can make progress without removing many vertices: it can eliminate a layer of permutation symmetry. A logarithmic bound on the total weight of these layers allows tests of constant size. Second, the auxiliary bipartite graphs arising in the symmetry-breaking step can be represented inside the current instance, after retaining a row decomposition when necessary. These recursive calls inherit the progress already made. Two further observations give the dependence on the degree. The recursive calls made by a local test check disjoint parts of the instance, so together they cost about as much as one call on the whole instance. And for graphs of maximum degree $d$, each large symmetric action that the algorithm must break acts on at most $d$ points. We present the algorithm through colorings, partitions, and bipartite graphs, and collect the permutation-group ingredients in one appendix. The result extends to string isomorphism and returns one isomorphism and generators for the full automorphism group.
item.dc:creator: MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Mahdi JafariRaviz

item.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2407.04898v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:20643-20659, 2024
item.dc:creator: Joon Suk Huh, Kirthevasan Kandasamy

item.title: Differential Privacy for Euclidean Jordan Algebra with Applications to Private Symmetric Cone Programming
item.description: arXiv:2509.16915v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study differentially private mechanisms for functions whose outputs lie in a Euclidean Jordan algebra. Euclidean Jordan algebras capture many important mathematical structures and form the foundation of linear programming, second-order cone programming, and semidefinite programming. Our main contribution is a generic Gaussian mechanism for such functions, with sensitivity measured in $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, and $\ell_\infty$ norms. Notably, this framework includes the important case where the function outputs are symmetric matrices, and sensitivity is measured in the Frobenius, nuclear, or spectral norm. We further derive private algorithms for solving symmetric cone programs under various settings, using a combination of the multiplicative weights update method and our generic Gaussian mechanism. As an application, we present differentially private algorithms for semidefinite programming, resolving a major open question posed by [Hsu, Roth, Roughgarden, and Ullman, ICALP 2014].
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Jianfei Xue, Lichen Zhang

item.title: A New Quantum Linear System Algorithm Beyond the Condition Number and Its Application to Solving Multivariate Polynomial Systems
item.description: arXiv:2510.05588v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a matrix $A$ of dimension $M \times N$ and a vector $\vec{b}$, the quantum linear system (QLS) problem asks for the preparation of a quantum state $|\vec{y}\rangle$ proportional to the solution of $A\vec{y} = \vec{b}$. Existing QLS algorithms have runtimes that scale linearly with the condition number $\kappa(A)$, the sparsity of $A$, and logarithmically with inverse precision, but often overlook structural properties of $\vec{b}$, whose alignment with $A$'s eigenspaces can greatly affect performance. In this work, we present a new QLS algorithm that explicitly leverages the structure of the right-hand side vector $\vec{b}$. The runtime of our algorithm depends polynomially on the sparsity of the augmented matrix $H = [A, -\vec{b}]$, the inverse precision, the $\ell_2$ norm of the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$, and a new instance-dependent parameter \[ ET= \sum_{i=1}^M p_i^2 \cdot d_i, \] where $\vec{p} = (AA^{\top})^+ \vec{b}$, and $d_i$ denotes the squared $\ell_2$ norm of the $i$-th row of $H$. We also introduce a structure-aware rescaling technique tailored to the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$. Unlike left preconditioning methods, which transform the linear system to $DA\vec{y} = D\vec{b}$, our approach applies a right rescaling matrix, reformulating the linear system as $AD\vec{z} = \vec{b}$. As an application of our instance-aware QLS algorithm and new rescaling scheme, we develop a quantum algorithm for solving multivariate polynomial systems in regimes where prior QLS-based methods fail. This yields an end-to-end framework applicable to a broad class of problems. In particular, we apply it to the maximum independent set (MIS) problem, formulated as a special case of a polynomial system, and show through detailed analysis that, under certain conditions, our quantum algorithm for MIS runs in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Jianqiang Li

item.title: EFX Need Not Exist
item.description: arXiv:2604.18216v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The existence of envy-free up to any good (EFX) allocations has long been a central open problem in discrete fair division. We resolve it in the negative by constructing a counterexample with three agents and eight goods. The instance is invariant under every simultaneous permutation of the agents and their associated good types, and this symmetry yields a short, self-contained proof of nonexistence. The counterexample can be realized with weighted-coverage, and hence submodular, valuations, and it extends to $n$ agents and $m$ goods for all $n\ge3$ and $m\ge n+5$. For three agents, eight goods is the minimum: every instance with three agents and at most seven goods admits an EFX allocation under arbitrary monotone valuations. The proof relies on a new analysis, valid for any number of goods, of when the invariant-based technique of [AACGMM25] produces an EFX allocation. This analysis strictly extends the class of MMS-feasible valuations. We also give explicit bounds for approximate EFX. For subadditive valuations, $\alpha$-EFX allocations need not exist for any $\alpha>2^{-1/6}\approx0.891$, and for submodular valuations for any $\alpha>0.958$. On the positive side, if two of three agents have arbitrary monotone valuations and the third has a subadditive valuation, there is always an allocation that is EFX for the first two and $2^{-1/3}$-EFX ($\approx0.794$) for the third. A first version of the counterexample and of the seven-goods result was obtained using SAT/SMT solving, and the insights it provided guided our classical, pen-and-paper proofs. We also describe the encoding, which we believe is a valuable tool in its own right: to our knowledge, this is the first use of SAT/SMT solving for EFX.
item.dc:creator: Hannaneh Akrami, Simon Mackenzie, Alexander Mayorov, Kurt Mehlhorn, Shreyas Srinivas, Mashbat Suzuki, Christoph Weidenbach

item.title: Strong Conflict-Free Vertex-Connection via Twin Cover: Kernelization and Chromatic Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2605.13299v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A strong conflict-free vertex connection coloring of a graph is a graph coloring for which, for every two distinct vertices of the graph, there exists a shortest path between them in which some color in said coloring appears only once. The strong conflict-free vertex connection number, denoted by $\operatorname{svcfc}(G)$, is the number of colors in the strong conflict-free vertex connection coloring with the smallest amount of colors out of all such colorings of $G$. We study the problem of deciding whether this number is at most some threshold together with the parameter twin cover. Our first result is that when we have given $(G,k)$ in which $k$ is some target number of colors and given some twin cover $X$ of $G$ which is of size $t$, there is a polynomial time reduction to an equivalent instance which has at most $\max\{2,t+k2^t\}$ vertices. This result allows us to give a kernel for Strong CFVC Number which is parameterized by $\operatorname{tc}(G)+k$, which implies that Strong CFVC Number is FPT w.r.t. the twin-cover number of $G$ so long as $k$ is fixed. Our second result is that if $G$ is a connected graph for which there exists a twin cover of size $t$, then $\chi(G)\le \operatorname{svcfc}(G)\le \chi(G)+t$. Our last result is an an exact expression for the chromatic number of graphs whose twin cover number is bounded. Namely, we show that for every proper coloring $\varphi$ of $G[X]$, the minimum number of colors needed to extend $\varphi$ to all of $G$ is $K_\varphi=\max_{S\subseteq X}(|\varphi(S)|+m(S))$, and hence $\chi(G)=\min_{\varphi\text{ proper on }G[X]} K_\varphi$. Our results indicate that twin cover is a meaningful parameter in the context of strong conflict-free vertex-connection, and show that once we have a fixed twin cover, the only difficulty left is in some additive threshold above the chromatic number.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 32nd International Computing and Combinatorics Conference (COCOON 2026), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16835, pp. 397-408, Springer (2027)
item.dc:creator: Samuel German

item.title: List coloring uncrowded hypergraphs at the shattering threshold
item.description: arXiv:2606.18048v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A foundational theorem of Ajtai, Koml\'os, Pintz, Spencer, and Szemer\'edi asserts that every $n$-vertex $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph (i.e., with girth at least $5$) of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ contains an independent set of size $cn(\log\Delta/\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. Improving an earlier bound of Frieze and Mubayi, Iliopoulos showed that every such hypergraph has list chromatic number at most $(1+o(1))(k-1)(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$. Determining the optimal leading constant in this bound remains a major open problem. A natural target, suggested by the coupon-collector heuristic, is $(k-1)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$, which also corresponds to the shattering threshold for coloring sparse random hypergraphs. Our main result shows that this target is attained: for every integer $k\ge2$, every $k$-uniform uncrowded hypergraph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ satisfies: $$\chi_\ell(\mathcal{H})\le(1+o(1))\Big((k-1)\frac{\Delta}{\log\Delta}\Big)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}.$$ In particular, this confirms a 2019 conjecture of Molloy for uncrowded hypergraphs. Building on this result, we prove that every $k$-uniform linear hypergraph of maximum degree at most $\Delta$ has chromatic number at most $(c_k+o(1))(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{\frac{1}{k-1}}$, where $c_k\to1$ as $k\to\infty$, thereby proving a conjecture of Verstra\"ete and Wilson on the independence number of linear hypergraphs in the stronger form of colorings. Our techniques also yield a palette sparsification theorem for uncrowded hypergraphs, partially answering a question of Casselgren and Eriksson.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Dhawan, Abhishek Methuku, Minh-Quan Vo

item.title: Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic
item.description: arXiv:2606.23727v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.
item.dc:creator: Ammar Daskin

item.title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.19510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^3 m/\varepsilon^5)$-query estimator of Meel et al. (2025), where $m \geq K$ is the total size of the token alphabet. (2) Under logit access, we use $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, and this is tight. (3) Under noisy logit access, we smoothly interpolate between the above two guarantees: if probability values are given to relative error $\sigma$, we use $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2\sigma^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithms, for example measuring the distance between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights. Our experiments highlight the robustness and practicality of estimating the total variation distance, which remains estimable where the KL divergence is infinite. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation.
item.dc:creator: Eric Price, Kevin Tian, Zhiyang Xun, Yusong Zhu

item.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
item.description: arXiv:2611.05726v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.
